tip: 'Avoir besoin' takes 'de', so the relative link is 'dont': 'la personne dont tu as besoin' = the person you need.
'Qui' is used for subjects: 'le restaurant fait' becomes 'le restaurant qui fait' = the restaurant that makes.
An if-clause with 'si' normally skips the conditional; the "would" verb sits in the other half: 'si j'avais' (had), 'je voyagerais' (would travel).
'Il faudrait que' softens 'il faut que' into a polite "you should", and the verb after it changes form: 'que tu prennes rendez-vous'.
'Plaire' flips the subject: 'ça me plairait' is literally "it would please me", not "I would like it". The thing you enjoy does the pleasing.
'N'avoir qu'à' means "to only have to", i.e. just: 'tu n'auras qu'à me passer un coup de fil' = you'll just have to give me a call.
Clothes "go" on you in French: 'te va très bien' means "suits you", from 'aller' (to go). 'Ça te va' = it looks good on you.
A scheduled event "has place" in French: 'avoir lieu' = to take place. 'La réunion aura lieu' = the meeting will take place.
Countries normally carry an article in French: 'le Japon', not just "Japan". You visit 'le Japon', 'la France', 'les États-Unis'.
France runs on the 24-hour clock: 'vingt heures' is 8 PM. Subtract 12 to get the evening time.
'Que' recycles the object into a connector: 'j'ai lu le livre' becomes 'le livre que j'ai lu' = the book (that) I read.
After 'devenir' or 'être' the profession drops its article: 'je deviendrais artiste', not 'un artiste' – 'il est médecin'.
'Eût' is a literary, old-style form of 'ait': 'bien qu'il eût raison' = 'bien qu'il ait raison' in everyday French – although he was right.
After 'dès que' and 'quand', French uses the future where English uses the present: 'dès qu'il fera beau' = as soon as the weather is (literally will be) nice.
French has two futures: 'ils travailleront' (simple future, felt as more distant or formal) and 'ils vont travailler' (near and planned). Both = they will work.
French marries reflexively: 'se marier', literally "to marry oneself". 'Ils se marieront' = they'll get married. Without 'se', 'marier' means to marry someone off.
No word for "on" with days: 'seront publiés vendredi' = will be published on Friday. Add 'le' – 'le vendredi' – and it means every Friday.
'Seras rentré' is a future perfect: "you will have gotten home". 'Rentrer' takes 'être' as its helper, hence 'seras', not 'auras'.
'Visiter' is for places, not people: 'nous visiterons la Bretagne'. To visit a person you say 'rendre visite à', not 'visiter quelqu'un'.
Age is something you have in French: 'elle aura trente ans' = literally "she will have thirty years". Using 'être' here is a classic English-speaker slip.
'Travail' becomes 'travaux' in the plural, and 'les travaux' usually means construction or renovation work: 'finirons les travaux' = will finish the building work.
After 'dès que', French uses the future where English keeps the present: 'elle sera prête' = literally "she will be ready". Both clauses go future.
'Aurais voulu' expresses regret about the past: 'j'aurais voulu être là' = I would have liked to be there, meaning I wish I had been but wasn't.
You take a decision in French, not make one: 'nous prendrons une décision' = we'll make a decision. Using 'faire' here would sound wrong.
'Décevoir' means to disappoint, not to deceive – a false friend. 'Je ne te décevrai pas' = I won't let you down. To deceive someone is 'tromper'.
'Essence' looks like the English "essence" but means gasoline: 'on va prendre de l'essence' = we'll get fuel.
'Manquer' reverses things: 'tu nous manqueras' = literally "you will be missing to us". The person missed is the subject, so 'tu me manques' means "I miss you".
Short adverbs like 'déjà' normally sit inside the two-part past: 'avais déjà vu' = had already seen, not 'avais vu déjà'.
'Réussir l'examen' means to pass the exam, not merely to succeed: 'qui ont réussi l'examen' = who passed it. To fail it is 'rater' or 'échouer à'.
'Demander' means to ask for, not to demand: 'demander une augmentation' = to ask for a raise. And you ask 'à' someone – 'demander à mon patron'.
